options.text: Lattice A has received more wennet-work relative to its tharl frame, but that work runs mostly tharl-to-tharl rather than chaining together; Lattice B has fewer wennets overall, but they have formed a longer chain that is comparatively independent of the frame.
Lattice A's higher cant means its wennet-work is also more independent of the frame than Lattice B's, since cant is just the whole-lattice version of pell.
A cant as high as Lattice A's should predict at least as long a pell as Lattice B's, so one of the two figures given must be a measurement error.
Lattice B must have had more wennets laid on it in total than Lattice A, since pell is the count that actually reflects how much wennet-laying has happened.

That a lattice's ostral/calvine class is partly a function of which counting convention the field has adopted, not a fixed property waiting to be read off — the underlying cant and pell barely change, but the classification flips depending on the rule applied.
That once Varrenby saw Emmerick's calculation on the Sellen lattice, she accepted her rule had been wrong and endorsed his mean-of-three-chains method instead.
That Emmerick's calculation shows Varrenby's original definitions of cant and pell were themselves mistaken, not just her classification boundary.
That the disagreement is a measurement error a more careful observer could resolve, since the lattice's true cant and pell are objectively fixed quantities.
No: wennets near the anchors are mostly spurs, so chains begun there end quickly, which is why the tessel trace underestimates pell less often, and by less, than the fenn trace does.
Yes: sampling more starting points gives the fenn trace a structurally better chance of finding the true longest chain, which matches why beginners prefer it.
No: but only because the tessel trace and the fenn trace always find the identical chain in practice, so neither method actually underestimates pell.
Yes: Mira Pole's objection that the tessel trace can never find a chain avoiding the middle shows the fenn trace is the more accurate method overall.

(1) is the Orrin pattern, which compares different lattices by how many vesks began them; (2) is the Tasker pattern, which follows one lattice's pell over time — the text treats these as distinct regularities, not two versions of the same finding.
(1) and (2) are the same regularity described twice, since both show pell decreasing under some condition.
(2) is the Orrin pattern and (1) is the Tasker pattern, since Orrin's original comparison concerned changes across a lattice's seasons rather than how many vesks began it.
(2) shows that moving air in draughty galleries physically stretches long wennet chains until they part, the same mechanism that later explained Orrin's multi-vesk finding.
A wennet: the classification depends on what its ends touch, not on thickness or tautness, and this thread touches only other threads at both ends.
A tharl, since thick, taut threads are tharls under the standard rule of thumb observers use to classify at a glance.
A spur, since it is a short thread whose two ends both lie near other threads rather than on the rock.
It cannot be classified without knowing its length, since tharls and wennets are distinguished mainly by how long and how taut they are.
Tamber — a break near a fastening indicates tamber, a gradual material change, and tamber is also the more common cause of wennet failure in a standing lattice, more common than pilse.
Pilse — beginners generally attribute broken wennets to pilse, the wear of crawling, and pilse is indeed the dominant cause of failure in a standing lattice.
Pilse — a break near a fastening is the sign of pilse, since that is where a snail's grip wears the thread as it crawls past.
Tamber — but pilse is actually the more common cause overall, and tamber only explains why some breaks happen near fastenings specifically.
The opposite holds: the higher a lattice hangs, the less likely it is to survive a flood season, and lattices close under the crown are lost most often of all.
None — height above the water is exactly what protects a lattice from flood loss, so the colleague's reasoning is sound.
The objection is that flood loss is mostly caused by silt film rather than by a lattice's height at all, so height is irrelevant to survival.
The objection is that a lattice's cant, not its height, determines flood survival, so height plays no role either way.
No — most lost lattices are lost to sudden violence, a flood or a fall of rock, and silt film accounts for only a small share of losses despite Varrenby's concern about it.
Yes — gradual threats like silt film accumulate unnoticed over many seasons, so they are the dominant, if underappreciated, cause of loss.
No — but only because rockfalls specifically outpace silt film, not because sudden violence in general is the dominant cause.
Yes — since a high cant is what determines whether a lattice survives a flood, gradual sediment buildup must be the deciding factor in the seasons between floods.

Lattice A's wennets have linked into longer wennet-to-wennet chains, while Lattice B's wennets more often run directly from tharl to tharl; both lattices have received the same amount of wennet-work relative to their frames.
Lattice A must have received more wennet-work overall than Lattice B, since a longer pell means more total wennets were laid on it.
Since the two lattices have equal cant, their pells should also be roughly equal, so the difference is most likely a counting error.
Lattice A must have more tharls than Lattice B, and that larger frame is what lets its chains run longer.

Ostral under Varrenby's original rule, because its single longest chain (9) exceeds twice its cant (8); calvine under current practice, because Emmerick's mean of the three longest chains (about 5.3) does not.
Ostral under both rules, since a chain of 9 is more than double a cant of 4 regardless of which method is used.
Calvine under both rules, since the mean of the three longest chains falls below twice the cant either way.
Ostral under current practice, but calvine under Varrenby's original rule.
No — wennets near the anchors are mostly spurs, so chains begun there end quickly, which is why the tessel trace underestimates pell less often and by less than the fenn trace does.
Yes — since the fenn trace samples more starting wennets, it is the more thorough method and should be preferred over the tessel trace.
No — the tessel trace is not really a shortcut at all, since it always finds the exact same pell that a full trace would find.
No — the fenn trace is actually the more reliable of the two, since chains beginning near an anchor tend to run especially long.

Finding 1 (the Orrin pattern) compares different lattices by how many vesks founded them and appears only in colder galleries; Finding 2 (the Tasker pattern) follows one lattice's pell over time and appears only in draughty galleries.
Both findings describe the same underlying process — pell falling because the moving air in a gallery physically stretches long wennet chains until they part.
Finding 1 and Finding 2 are the same regularity studied at two different scales — one measuring the group of founders, one measuring a single lattice.
Finding 1 holds everywhere, while Finding 2 only appears in warmer galleries.
Nothing conclusive — a thread's kind is defined by what its two ends touch, not by its thickness or slackness, so the appearance-based shortcut can mis-sort exactly the lattices where it fails.
The observer has correctly identified a wennet, since fineness and slackness are the defining features of that category of thread.
The observer has identified a spur, a distinct third category of thread separate from tharls and wennets.
The observer has at least ruled out that the thread is a tharl, since a tharl must be thick and taut by definition.
Tamber — a gradual change in the hardened mucus — because tamber breaks occur near a fastening, while pilse (wear from crawling) breaks occur near a wennet's middle.
Pilse, because most broken wennets in a standing lattice are caused by snails wearing them down as they crawl across.
Pilse, because a break near a fastening is where a crawling snail would grip on to cross from one thread to another.
Neither can be determined — break location doesn't reliably indicate cause once a wennet has already parted.
Lattice X — height above the water correlates with greater flood risk, and lattices closest to the crown, the highest position available, are lost most often of all.
Lattice Y — hanging closer to the crown puts it farther from the rising floodwater, so it should be safer.
Both are equally likely to survive, since flood risk depends only on the gallery's overall dampness category, not on where within it a lattice hangs.
Lattice X, but only because lattices near the waterline tend to have higher cant, and it is the higher cant that protects them.
Most lost lattices are lost to sudden violence — a scouring flood or a rockfall — while silt film accounts for only a small share of losses; effort would be better aimed at flood and rockfall risk.
None — silt film is confirmed as the dominant cause of lattice loss, so the group's priority is well-founded.
The data actually shows that gradual threats in general, including silt film, destroy more lattices than sudden violent events do, so any gradual-threat program would help.
The group should instead focus on wennet failure from tamber, since that is the field's leading cause of lattice loss overall.
